Docs/Replay/Guide

Replay

Fixed-roster P2P admission

4 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Godot integrationLifecycle and boundariesEvidence

This package authenticates a participant against a trusted match provider before a physical connection is bound to a P2P roster slot. It does not supply gameplay state, elect a simulation authority or choose a winning checksum.

Match names a session, content version, epoch and ordered roster of 2–8 nonzero, unique member IDs. Registry is owned by the provider and holds the current credential incarnation, secret key and enabled flag for each member. Clients get the match description and only their own credential. Validate the complete registry with registry_valid before publishing it. Stable member order determines player roles; the first member may create the signaling room and the others may join.

proof produces a fixed 116-byte request. It binds the create/join role, session, epoch, member/incarnation, ordered-match SHA-256 digest and 16-byte connection challenge under a domain-separated HMAC-SHA256 using the member's 32-byte key. verify checks the registry, exact identity, enabled status, role, challenge, MAC and complete match scope. The domain is replay-p2p-admission-v1; this proof is separate from the authority-lease rendezvous proof. A room code is the hexadecimal match digest, not a credential. No secret key is sent in the proof.

The verifier is stateless. The signaling frontend must create a cryptographically random challenge per connection, consume it once and enforce a deadline. It must assign the sender identity itself when forwarding signaling messages. Authenticate the provider through a trusted transport such as verified WSS for deployment; client proof does not authenticate an arbitrary server to the client.

Godot integration#

The existing bounded Rendezvous frontend implements the challenge lifecycle, rate/size limits and continuation reservations. It now accepts an explicit Rendezvous_Provider; ordinary rendezvous_init keeps the authority Service policy. For a P2P registry:

Odin
provider := rgd.rendezvous_p2p_provider(&registry, clock)
cfg := rgd.DEFAULT_RENDEZVOUS_CONFIG
cfg.mesh = true
ok := rgd.rendezvous_provider_init(&frontend, provider, &websocket, cfg)

The frontend borrows the registry, clock and socket. Keep their addresses stable. Poll the socket, route text messages through rendezvous_receive, and pump the frontend as documented in Rendezvous. Full-mesh introductions and signaling are opt-in; ordinary authority rooms remain stars.

The client owns a stable Rtc_P2P_Auth{match, identity, key} and opens with rtc_p2p_config. Peer introductions carry member and incarnation as exact 64-bit hex values. require_identity refuses missing/invalid metadata; rtc_peer_identity(&rtc, physical_id) exposes the verified introduction only for a connected peer on an authenticated signaling connection. Verify that member against the expected roster, create the logical-to-physical Remap, then initialize or reconnect the P2P runner. A fresh physical ID alone never establishes membership.

Lifecycle and boundaries#

Changing credential incarnation invalidates old admission proofs while retaining the same match code and stable member roster. Disabling a credential removes its signaling permission. The provider owns durable credential storage, monotonic incarnation registration, revocation policy and secure personal-key distribution; this package does not implement an account database or public provisioning UI. Registry updates must happen at an externally synchronized boundary.

Admission authenticates connection establishment. Established direct gameplay channels can outlive signaling loss. Removing signaling permission alone is not a complete policy for ejecting a player from an already connected match; the application/provider must also fence its gameplay transport or terminate that fixed-roster match. Changing the roster requires a new match contract. There is no claim that a peer can be trusted to simulate honestly merely because it authenticated.

The signaling frontend retains the first member as the room creator. Its browser process may now return from a compatible archive while peers retain their runners. The creator keeps numeric RTC ID 1; the survivor detects the new connection generation and the transport wrappers discard retired buffered work. This requires the same live provider/match scope; it does not elect a different roster member to replace the creator or recover its missing inputs. Fresh participants cannot steal an existing continuation reservation using only a member key. After the configured reservation expires they may obtain a new ID with a fresh challenge; the P2P runner still requires a compatible durable input archive.

Evidence#

tests/replay_p2p_admission/run.sh checks valid roles and rejection of changed scope/roster, key, challenge, incarnation and malformed registries. The real Godot service_run.sh admits three members, checks exact identity introductions, client-to-client signaling and sender-spoof overwriting, and rejects five bad admission attempts using independently constructed Node HMACs.

web_run.sh imports personal fixture credentials in separate Chrome processes, then performs the Duel's Save & pause, SIGKILL and fresh-browser archive rejoin for the joining player and the creator in separate scenarios. The existing authority-based RTC service, signaling continuation/expiry, P2P core and plain browser fault gates also pass. See the recorded results. The service fixture binds loopback and contains published test keys. Public WSS, account provisioning, authenticated spectator roles and broader platform acceptance remain open work.
